lines.text: Hi, I'm Sindy! In this episode, we go from an empty machine to a running Slurm cluster, and back again.
Say you're a research software engineer with a fresh batch script. You'd like to watch it run on a real Slurm cluster, today.
All you need is a Linux machine with Docker, plus sind itself, a single binary. sind needs no root privileges of its own.
Here's the plan: install sind, check the host with sind doctor, create a cluster and submit the job, then SSH in and clean up.
First, download the binary from the latest release. This one is for Intel and AMD machines, and there's one for ARM too.
Before you install it, verify it. The release carries a build attestation, and the GitHub CLI checks that the sind release workflow made this file.
Then install it for your user alone, into the local bin directory. No root needed.
If your shell can't find sind, log out and back in. Most distributions only put that directory on your path if it exists at login.
Prefer a tool manager, or building from source with Go? The installation guide covers both.
Next, ask sind doctor whether the host is ready. It looks at the Docker version and daemon mode, where the daemon runs, and the cgroup setup.
Every line starts with a check mark, so we're good to go. If a check fails, sind doctor tells you how to fix it.
Time for the cluster! Run sind create cluster. With no options, you get one controller and one worker, in a cluster named default.
sind is silent when all goes well, so let's ask: sind get clusters reports it as running.
And sind get nodes goes one level deeper: every node container, with its host name and IP address.
One detail makes testing easy. sind mounts your current directory on every node, as the data directory.
So a script you save here is right there on the controller and the worker, and so is its output.
Let's write a tiny job script. It prints the host name of its node, then sleeps for thirty seconds.
Submit it with sind exec, which runs sbatch on the controller. Slurm answers with the job ID.
Once the job completes, its output file is right here in your directory. Hello from worker zero!
Want to look around on a node yourself? sind ssh worker zero logs you in there, as root.
Your shell starts in the home directory, not in the data directory.
Back on your machine, sind delete cluster removes the cluster when you're done.
And with the last cluster gone, sind also cleans up the shared network, DNS and SSH services.
Let's recap. Run sind doctor first, so you know the host is ready.
One command creates a cluster, and one more deletes it.
And your current directory becomes the data directory on every node, so your jobs see your files.
Next up: inside a sind cluster, with its roles, networks and DNS. See you there!
